analysis.one_liner: Requires your explicit permission before credit bureaus can sell your credit report to anyone.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Banking Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, credit bureaus can share your credit report with lenders, insurers, and marketers unless you take the step of opting out. This bill would flip that: bureaus could only share your report after you give informed, verified permission, except for firm offers of credit or insurance. It would also ban bureaus from charging you fees for these activities, require them to take concrete steps to prevent data breaches, and order the Government Accountability Office to study what further protections consumer files need [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers gain control over who sees their credit file, plus protection from data breaches and from fees charged for accessing or freezing their own reports. Identity theft victims and people tired of prescreened marketing offers benefit most [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the default from opt-out to affirmative informed consent: a credit bureau may furnish your report for credit or insurance purposes only after you agree and the bureau verifies your identity [S2][S3].
Credit bureaus could not charge consumers any fee for activities under the bill, covering consent management and report access [S2][S3].
Bureaus would have to use commercially reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized access to consumer reports, including following Gramm-Leach-Bliley data security standards [S3].
The Government Accountability Office would have to study and report within a year on what additional protections consumer files need [S2][S3].

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would have to write rules within 270 days, including a cost-free, convenient method (phone or secure electronic) for consumers to give or revoke consent, implemented within one business day [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus lose revenue from selling report access and prescreened marketing lists without consent, and bear compliance costs for identity verification and data security. Lenders and insurers that rely on prescreened firm offers would reach fewer prospects unless consumers opt in [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Requiring verified consent before a report can be pulled could add friction to applying for credit or insurance, potentially slowing approvals for consumers who want quick decisions [S3].
Prescreened firm offers of credit and insurance — which can expose consumers to competing offers — would require opt-in consent, so consumers who never opt in would stop receiving them [S2][S3].

Compliance costs for identity verification and one-business-day implementation of consent changes would fall on the bureaus and could be reflected in their pricing to lenders, with some possibility of passthrough to borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is privacy and data security versus convenience: consumers gain control over their most sensitive financial data and relief from fees, at the cost of one extra consent step when applying for credit. The strongest objection — slower credit approvals — is mitigated by the bill's requirement that the CFPB write rules allowing consent to cover multiple users for a set period [S3]. On balance the consumer benefits outweigh the friction costs, though the bill relies heavily on CFPB rulemaking to work smoothly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, with Senator Chris Van Hollen as cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day [S1][S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and the lenders and insurers that buy prescreened marketing lists are better off, because the current opt-out system — where they can access consumer data unless a consumer actively objects — remains the law.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumer Credit Control Act and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators, both Democrats, ever supported the bill on the record, and no vote was ever held, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition never showed.

industries.note: Their business is selling consumer report access and prescreened lists; the bill flips the default to consumer consent, bans fees charged to consumers, and imposes data-security obligations. Consumers currently bear breach risks and fees the bill would eliminate.

industries.industry: Lenders and insurers using prescreened marketing
industries.note: Prescreened firm offers would still be allowed but only with verified consumer consent, shrinking the prospect lists these firms buy. Their actual underwriting would continue with consent obtained at application.
